public_rationale: On the ordinary reading about action taken, almost nothing understates the response. Before the post, the FCC had applied robocall protections to AI voices, Minnesota had put election-deepfake restrictions into effect, and Google had made experimental image watermarking available. These were concrete legal and technical measures. They do not establish that the response was adequate or that misinformation's impact had substantially declined.
limitations: The outcome depends on reading done as action implemented rather than harm demonstrably prevented.
The technical deployment was experimental and limited to supported images.
State legislation does not establish congressional action.
No inference is made that the misinformation problem was solved.

statement.excerpt: Over a year ago in The Atlantic, I urged that we come up with laws and new technological responses to blunt the impact of AI-generated misinformation. So far almost nothing has been done.
statement.document_title: We can’t trust the fox to guard the henhouse, especially when it comes to AI

evidence.explanation: The ruling applied existing consent and disclosure protections to AI-generated voice calls and became effective on release. It was a concrete federal response relevant to deceptive impersonation calls, subject to statutory exemptions.

evidence.excerpt: This section is effective August 1, 2023, and applies to crimes committed on or after that date.
evidence.locator: Section 2, Use of Deep Fake Technology to Influence an Election, effective-date provision
evidence.publisher: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes
evidence.explanation: Section 2 criminalized specified nonconsensual dissemination of deepfakes within 90 days of an election when intended to injure a candidate or influence the result. This enacted, operative restriction directly addressed election misinformation.
